plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single three-dimensional drawing of a right circular cone, shaded in translucent teal with its apex at the top and an elliptical base at the bottom, cut by four dashed lines that each mark a different slicing plane. Near the apex a short, nearly horizontal dashed segment crossing a lightly shaded band is labeled 'Circle'. Below it a dashed line tilted modestly from horizontal passes through both sides of the cone and is labeled 'Ellipse'. A steeper dashed line runs from the upper left side of the cone down through the base and carries the label 'Parabola'. The fourth dashed line is nearly vertical, dropping through the right portion of the cone to the base, and is labeled 'Hyperbola'. Each cut has a correspondingly shaded region rendered inside the translucent solid, so the section surface itself is visible rather than just the cutting line, and all four labels are stacked along the right edge. Steepening the cut progressively from horizontal to vertical is the entire visual argument: one surface yields all four curves depending only on the inclination of the plane. The drawing collects the family of paths that an inverse-square force allows, the closed circle and ellipse alongside the open parabola and hyperbola.

elements: right circular cone, apex at top, translucent teal surface
elliptical base rim at the bottom of the cone
apex point marker at the top
four dashed cutting-plane trace lines, each at a different inclination, stacked from near-horizontal (top) to near-vertical (bottom-right)
four shaded semi-transparent section regions inside the cone, one per cut
active highlighted intersection curve (the conic produced by the current plane)
label 'Circle' at upper right next to the near-horizontal cut
label 'Ellipse' at right next to the modestly tilted cut
label 'Parabola' at right next to the steep cut
label 'Hyperbola' at lower right next to the near-vertical cut

interactions.label: Plane inclination θ
interactions.teaches: Steepening one cutting plane continuously morphs the highlighted section from a closed circle, to a closed ellipse, to an open parabola, to an open hyperbola — proving a single cone generates every inverse-square orbit family purely by inclination

interactions.label: Conic section
interactions.teaches: Selecting a named cut snaps the plane to that canonical inclination and brightens its intersection while the other three fade, clarifying which closed or open path belongs to each slice
Rotating the cone reveals that each dashed line is the edge-on view of a full slicing plane, and that the shaded band is the actual planar intersection surface, not just a line

demo_steps.title: Circle (θ = 0°)
demo_steps.narration: A horizontal plane near the apex cuts a perfect circle — the only closed section perpendicular to the cone axis.

demo_steps.title: Ellipse (θ ≈ 30°)
demo_steps.narration: Tilting the plane so it still crosses every generator on this nappe yields a closed ellipse — the bound-orbit family.

demo_steps.title: Parabola (θ ≈ 69°)
demo_steps.narration: At the critical angle where the plane runs parallel to one generator, the section opens into a parabola — the escape trajectory.

demo_steps.title: Hyperbola (θ ≈ 80°)
demo_steps.narration: Steepening past the generator angle makes the plane cut both nappes, producing an open hyperbola — the unbound flyby path.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Cone: apex at world (0, +2, 0), circular base radius 1.5 centered at (0, -2, 0); base drawn as an ellipse by the axonometric pose. Radius profile r(y) = 0.375*(2 - y). Half-angle alpha = atan(1.5/4) ≈ 20.56°. Cutting plane tilted about the x-axis with normal n = (0, cosθ, sinθ) passing through P0 ≈ (0, 0.3, 0); θ is the slider value in degrees. Classification vs axis: circle at θ=0; ellipse for θ < 90°-alpha (≈69.4°); parabola at θ ≈ 69.4°; hyperbola for θ > 69.4°. Compute each intersection curve numerically by sampling the cone lateral surface and keeping points where |n·(p-P0)| < eps, then draw as a bright line. Cone surface teal #6fbdbd at ~0.35 opacity; section regions darker teal-grey #4a7d7d at ~0.5 opacity; active intersection curve near-black #1a1a1a; dashed trace lines black; labels black text stacked down the right edge at increasing height matching each cut. Four faint planes always visible (matching source), the active one emphasized.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the cone as a THREE.ConeGeometry (open-ended) with a transparent MeshBasicMaterial (double-sided) so the interior sections show through. Render the base rim as a separate line loop. For each named cut precompute its intersection polyline once; the slider recomputes a single 'live' intersection each frame by intersecting the plane with the cone parametric surface (sample azimuth 0..2π and height, test plane sign). Toggle sets the slider to the canonical θ for that name and sets which precomputed section is bright vs faded. Keep labels as screen-space sprites anchored to the right side so they stay legible during orbit.

authoredContext:
One of the real triumphs of Newton’s law of universal gravitation, with the force proportional to the inverse of the distance squared, is that when it is combined with his second law, the solution for the path of any satellite is a conic section. Every path taken by m is one of the four conic sections: a circle or an ellipse for bound or closed orbits, or a parabola or hyperbola for unbounded or open orbits. These conic sections are shown in the figure.

All motion caused by an inverse square force is one of the four conic sections and is determined by the energy and direction of the moving body.

A cone and its conic sections is shown. At the top a horizontal cut is shaded and a dashed line shown across the shading. This section is labeled circle. Below this a diagonal cut and line are shown. The line and cut intersect the sides of the cone. This section is labeled ellipse. Next is a diagonal cut and line that intersect the sides and the bottom of the cone and are labeled parabola. The last section is a vertical line and shaded cut labeled hyperbola

If the total energy is negative, then 0≤e<1, and the equation represents a bound or closed orbit of either an ellipse or a circle, where e=0. [You can see from the equation that for e=0, r=α, and hence the radius is constant.] For ellipses, the eccentricity is related to how oblong the ellipse appears. A circle has zero eccentricity, whereas a very long, drawn-out ellipse has an eccentricity near one.

demo_steps.title: Parabola (θ ≈ 69°)
demo_steps.narration: At the critical angle where the plane runs parallel to one generator, the section opens into a parabola — the escape trajectory.

demo_steps.title: Hyperbola (θ ≈ 80°)
demo_steps.narration: Steepening past the generator angle makes the plane cut both nappes, producing an open hyperbola — the unbound flyby path.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Cone: apex at world (0, +2, 0), circular base radius 1.5 centered at (0, -2, 0); base drawn as an ellipse by the axonometric pose. Radius profile r(y) = 0.375*(2 - y). Half-angle alpha = atan(1.5/4) ≈ 20.56°. Cutting plane tilted about the x-axis with normal n = (0, cosθ, sinθ) passing through P0 ≈ (0, 0.3, 0); θ is the slider value in degrees. Classification vs axis: circle at θ=0; ellipse for θ < 90°-alpha (≈69.4°); parabola at θ ≈ 69.4°; hyperbola for θ > 69.4°. Compute each intersection curve numerically by sampling the cone lateral surface and keeping points where |n·(p-P0)| < eps, then draw as a bright line. Cone surface teal #6fbdbd at ~0.35 opacity; section regions darker teal-grey #4a7d7d at ~0.5 opacity; active intersection curve near-black #1a1a1a; dashed trace lines black; labels black text stacked down the right edge at increasing height matching each cut. Four faint planes always visible (matching source), the active one emphasized.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the cone as a THREE.ConeGeometry (open-ended) with a transparent MeshBasicMaterial (double-sided) so the interior sections show through. Render the base rim as a separate line loop. For each named cut precompute its intersection polyline once; the slider recomputes a single 'live' intersection each frame by intersecting the plane with the cone parametric surface (sample azimuth 0..2π and height, test plane sign). Toggle sets the slider to the canonical θ for that name and sets which precomputed section is bright vs faded. Keep labels as screen-space sprites anchored to the right side so they stay legible during orbit.

plan.authoredPrompt: This figure is a single three-dimensional drawing of a right circular cone, shaded in translucent teal with its apex at the top and an elliptical base at the bottom, cut by four dashed lines that each mark a different slicing plane. Near the apex a short, nearly horizontal dashed segment crossing a lightly shaded band is labeled 'Circle'. Below it a dashed line tilted modestly from horizontal passes through both sides of the cone and is labeled 'Ellipse'. A steeper dashed line runs from the upper left side of the cone down through the base and carries the label 'Parabola'. The fourth dashed line is nearly vertical, dropping through the right portion of the cone to the base, and is labeled 'Hyperbola'. Each cut has a correspondingly shaded region rendered inside the translucent solid, so the section surface itself is visible rather than just the cutting line, and all four labels are stacked along the right edge. Steepening the cut progressively from horizontal to vertical is the entire visual argument: one surface yields all four curves depending only on the inclination of the plane. The drawing collects the family of paths that an inverse-square force allows, the closed circle and ellipse alongside the open parabola and hyperbola.
plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for cutting-plane angle: the learner steepens the plane through the cone, the highlighted section morphs from circle to ellipse to parabola to hyperbola, showing how one cone generates all four orbit families by changing inclination.
- Toggle between named conic cuts: the learner selects Circle, Ellipse, Parabola, or Hyperbola, the matching plane and intersection are emphasized while the others fade, clarifying which closed or open path corresponds to each slice.
